title: How grieving changes the brain, with Mary-Frances O’Connor, PhD

sentences.en: Few of us will make it through life without losing someone we love.
sentences.zh: 我们大多数人一生中都难免会经历失去挚爱的痛苦。

sentences.en: Grief, it's been said, is the cost of love.
sentences.zh: 人们常说，悲伤是爱的代价。

sentences.en: The yearning and sadness we feel after someone dies is the price we sometimes pay for the close relationships that we treasure.
sentences.zh: 亲人离世后我们感受到的渴望与哀伤，有时正是我们为珍视的亲密关系所付出的代价。

sentences.en: Some people are resilient after loss, able to cope with their acute grief and eventually adjust to life without their loved one.
sentences.zh: 有些人失去亲人后具有韧性，能够应对剧烈的悲伤，并最终适应没有挚爱陪伴的生活。

sentences.en: Others, meanwhile, find themselves unable to do so.
sentences.zh: 而另一些人则发现自己无法做到这一点。

sentences.en: Over the past two decades, researchers have begun using the tools of modern neuroscience to better understand why that is,
sentences.zh: 在过去的二十年里，研究人员开始利用现代神经科学工具来更好地理解其中的原因，

sentences.en: and more broadly, to understand what happens to our brains and bodies during the grieving process, and how best to help people mourning the death of a loved one.
sentences.zh: 更广泛地说，是为了了解在悲伤过程中我们的大脑和身体会发生什么，以及如何最好地帮助那些哀悼挚爱离世的人。

sentences.en: So what makes someone more or less resilient in the face of loss?
sentences.zh: 那么，是什么让人在面对失去时表现出更强或更弱的韧性呢？

sentences.en: How is grieving related to depression, and how is it different?
sentences.zh: 悲伤与抑郁有何关联？它们又有何不同？

sentences.en: What happens to our brains when we are grieving?
sentences.zh: 当我们感到悲伤时，大脑会发生什么？

sentences.en: Is there effective therapy for grief?
sentences.zh: 是否有针对悲伤的有效疗法？

sentences.en: Is it possible to experience actual grief over the death of a celebrity, and how is that grief different from grief over the loss of a loved one?
sentences.zh: 一个人是否可能对名人的去世产生真正的悲伤？这种悲伤与失去挚爱所带来的悲伤有何不同？

sentences.en: How can we best support people when they are grieving?
sentences.zh: 当人们处于悲伤中时，我们该如何给予最好的支持？

sentences.en: Welcome to Speaking of Psychology, the flagship podcast of the American Psychological Association that examines the links between psychological science and everyday life.
sentences.zh: 欢迎收听《心理学谈话》，这是美国心理学会的旗舰播客，旨在探讨心理科学与日常生活之间的联系。

sentences.en: I'm Kim Mills.
sentences.zh: 我是金·米尔斯。

sentences.en: Our guest today is Dr. Mary Frances O'Connor, an associate professor of psychology at the University of Arizona, where she studies grief and grieving.
sentences.zh: 我们今天的嘉宾是亚利桑那大学心理学副教授玛丽·弗朗西斯·奥康纳博士，她专门研究悲伤与哀悼。

sentences.en: She uses methods including brain imaging and studying immune system responses to investigate how grieving affects us both psychologically and physiologically.
sentences.zh: 她利用脑成像和研究免疫系统反应等方法，调查悲伤如何在心理和生理上影响我们。

sentences.en: She is an expert in complicated grief, a clinical condition in which people don't adjust to acute feelings of grief.
sentences.zh: 她是复杂性悲伤方面的专家，这是一种临床病症，患者无法适应剧烈的悲伤情绪。

sentences.en: In addition to her many scientific publications, she is author of the recent book,
sentences.zh: 除了发表过许多科学著作外，她还是近期出版的新书的作者，

sentences.en: The Grieving Brain,
sentences.zh: 《悲伤的大脑》，

sentences.en: The Surprising Science of How We Learn from Love and Loss.
sentences.zh: 《关于我们如何从爱与失去中学习的惊人科学》。

sentences.en: Thank you for joining us today, Dr. O'Connor.
sentences.zh: 感谢您今天加入我们的节目，奥康纳博士。

sentences.en: It's so good to be here.
sentences.zh: 很高兴来到这里。

sentences.en: Thanks.
sentences.zh: 谢谢。

sentences.en: One of the points that you make in your book is that grieving is actually a form of learning.
sentences.zh: 您在书中提到的一个观点是，悲伤实际上是一种学习形式。

sentences.en: Can you explain what that means?
sentences.zh: 您能解释一下这意味着什么吗？

sentences.en: I don't think most people think of grieving in that way.
sentences.zh: 我想大多数人并不认为悲伤是这样的。

sentences.en: This has really come about from years now, studying grief and grieving, and reading a lot of studies about what happens when we experience the death of a loved one.
sentences.zh: 这确实源于多年来对悲伤和哀悼的研究，以及阅读了大量关于我们经历挚爱离世时会发生什么的研究。

sentences.en: And it really has struck me that grieving can be thought of as a form of learning.
sentences.zh: 我确实深受触动，认为悲伤可以被视为一种学习形式。

sentences.en: This is, you know, in a few different ways we can think of it.
sentences.zh: 你知道，我们可以从几个不同的角度来思考这个问题。

sentences.en: One is that after we experience something as difficult as, you know, our one and only passing away, we really have to figure out how do I live in the world now?
sentences.zh: 其一，在经历了像我们唯一的亲人离世这样困难的事情后，我们真的必须弄清楚：我现在该如何在这个世界上生活？

sentences.en: What does it mean to retire when, you know, this person that I've been going to do this with for decades, is no longer going to do that with me.
sentences.zh: 当你几十年来一直计划一起退休的那个人，不再能和你一起实现这个目标时，退休意味着什么？

sentences.en: So part of it is learning to be in the world as a person who carries this absence with them.
sentences.zh: 所以，其中一部分是学习如何作为一个带着这种缺失感的人在世界上生活。

sentences.en: But even at a smaller level, you can think about all the tiny little habits that we have to change.
sentences.zh: 但即使在更小的层面上，你也可以想想我们必须改变的所有细微习惯。

sentences.en: This is that feeling of, you know, the experience of picking up the phone to call them because something has happened.
sentences.zh: 这就是那种感觉，你知道，比如发生什么事时，习惯性地拿起电话想打给他们。

sentences.en: And then, of course, realizing that we can't call them.
sentences.zh: 然后，当然，意识到我们不能再打给他们了。

sentences.en: So all those little habits and predictions that we have to learn in a new way.
sentences.zh: 所以，所有那些细小的习惯和预测，我们都必须以一种新的方式去学习。

sentences.en: Let's talk about the difference between grief and grieving since we're going to be using those terms a lot as we talk.
sentences.zh: 我们来谈谈“悲伤（grief）”和“哀悼（grieving）”之间的区别，因为我们在谈话中会经常用到这两个词。

sentences.en: And you've made the point that they're not interchangeable terMs.
sentences.zh: 您曾指出它们并不是可以互换的术语。

sentences.en: I found it to be helpful in a scientific way to distinguish between grief and grieving.
sentences.zh: 我发现在科学层面上区分“悲伤”和“哀悼”是有帮助的。

sentences.en: And then as I did that, came to find that other people found it useful as well.
sentences.zh: 当我这样做之后，我发现其他人也觉得这很有用。

sentences.en: So grief really is that feeling that you have, the sort of intensity that just overwhelms you and that sort of momentary experience.
sentences.zh: “悲伤”确实是你所拥有的那种感觉，那种让你不知所措的强度，以及那种瞬间的体验。

sentences.en: Grieving, on the other hand, is the way that grief changes over time without ever actually going away.
sentences.zh: 而“哀悼”则是悲伤随着时间推移而发生变化的方式，尽管它从未真正消失。

sentences.en: So for example, the first hundred times you get knocked off your feeling by that feeling of grief, that wave of grief.
sentences.zh: 举个例子，前一百次你被那种悲伤的感觉、那阵悲伤的浪潮击倒时，

sentences.en: The hundred and first time, it may be just as awful, but it may also be familiar so that now you may have some ways to comfort yourself
sentences.zh: 第一百零一次，它可能依然糟糕，但可能也变得熟悉了，所以现在你可能有一些安慰自己的方法，

sentences.en: or you may know how to reach out to someone in that moment.
sentences.zh: 或者你知道在那一刻如何向他人求助。

sentences.en: So even though the feeling hasn't necessarily changed, our relationship to the feeling changes over time.
sentences.zh: 所以，即使这种感觉本身不一定改变，我们与这种感觉的关系也会随着时间而改变。

sentences.en: And the reason that people have found this to be useful, I think, is if we expect that we're not going to feel grief in the future, that somehow it's going to be over,
sentences.zh: 我认为人们觉得这很有用的原因在于，如果我们期望未来不会再感到悲伤，认为它总会结束，

sentences.en: then we'll be disappointed if years later, even decades later, we come across something and suddenly we get all teared up and have that wave of grief.
sentences.zh: 那么当多年甚至几十年后，我们偶然遇到某件事，突然泪流满面并再次感受到那阵悲伤时，我们会感到失望。

sentences.en: That doesn't mean that we've done anything wrong in our grieving process.
sentences.zh: 这并不意味着我们在哀悼过程中做错了什么。

sentences.en: It just means that in that moment, we're aware of the loss of something really important.
sentences.zh: 这只是意味着在那一刻，我们意识到了失去某件非常重要事物的痛苦。

sentences.en: What is the relationship between grief and depression?
sentences.zh: 悲伤与抑郁之间的关系是什么？

sentences.en: And can a person grieve without being depressed?
sentences.zh: 一个人在不抑郁的情况下可以感到悲伤吗？

sentences.en: The heart of grieving really is around yearning, yearning for that person to be back or for things to be back the way they were before.
sentences.zh: 悲伤的核心其实是渴望，渴望那个人回来，或者渴望一切回到从前的样子。

sentences.en: And we know now from both diagnostic clinical science, but also brain imaging work, that grief and depression are not the same thing.
sentences.zh: 我们现在从诊断临床科学和脑成像研究中得知，悲伤和抑郁不是一回事。

sentences.en: So we can have both grief and we can have depression just in the same way you could have depression and anxiety, say, for example.
sentences.zh: 所以我们既可以有悲伤，也可以有抑郁，就像你可能同时患有抑郁症和焦虑症一样。

sentences.en: But you can have one without the other.
sentences.zh: 但你也可以只拥有其中一种，而没有另一种。

sentences.en: In depression, the feelings are usually more global.
sentences.zh: 在抑郁症中，这种感觉通常更全面、更广泛。

sentences.en: So while I may feel awful that my loved one isn't here anymore, with depression, I will probably feel awful about a lot of things.
sentences.zh: 所以，虽然我可能会因为挚爱不在了而感到难过，但在抑郁状态下，我可能会对很多事情都感到难过。

sentences.en: I'll feel guilty about things I've done in the past and worried about the way I'm interacting with people at work and also concerned about the things
sentences.zh: 我会为过去做过的事情感到内疚，担心自己与同事的互动方式，也会担心那些

sentences.en: that I've never fulfilled in my life that I should have done.
sentences.zh: 我一生中从未实现、本该完成的事情。

sentences.en: You know, depression tends to be quite global.
sentences.zh: 你知道，抑郁往往是相当全面的。

sentences.en: Grieving really focuses on that loved one.
sentences.zh: 而哀悼则真正聚焦于那位挚爱。

sentences.en: It's really about, I need this person to be back.
sentences.zh: 它真的是关于：我需要这个人回来。

sentences.en: I can't make it without this person with me.
sentences.zh: 没有这个人，我无法生活下去。

sentences.en: And so it's a slightly different experience.
sentences.zh: 所以这是一种略有不同的体验。

sentences.en: You wrote in your new book about how losing a loved one can feel like losing a part of yourself.
sentences.zh: 您在书中写道，失去挚爱感觉就像失去了自己的一部分。

sentences.en: And you tied that in with the work of Arthur Aaron, who is another psychologist who was recently on this podcaSt.
sentences.zh: 您将其与亚瑟·阿伦（Arthur Aaron）的工作联系起来，他是另一位最近参加过本播客的心理学家。

sentences.en: Can you talk about that connection?
sentences.zh: 您能谈谈这种联系吗？

sentences.en: Why do we experience loss this way?
sentences.zh: 为什么我们会有这种失去感？

sentences.en: Well, to think about what happens when we lose a loved one, you have to first recognize that the brain encodes a bond when you fall in love with your spouse or with your child,
sentences.zh: 嗯，要思考当我们失去挚爱时会发生什么，你首先必须认识到，当你爱上你的配偶或孩子时，大脑会编码一种纽带，

sentences.en: the brain encodes this bond.
sentences.zh: 大脑会编码这种纽带。

sentences.en: Essentially, it creates a we, not just a you and a me, but it creates a we of overlapping experience.
sentences.zh: 本质上，它创造了一个“我们”，不仅仅是你和我，而是创造了一个重叠体验的“我们”。

sentences.en: Um, and, and because of that, then when a loved one is no longer there, we actually experience it as, as part of us is missing, right?
sentences.zh: 嗯，正因为如此，当挚爱不在时，我们实际上会体验到仿佛我们的一部分缺失了，对吧？

sentences.en: So at a, at a very neural encoded level, our representation of the we has a hole in it.
sentences.zh: 所以在神经编码的层面上，我们对“我们”的表征中出现了一个空洞。

sentences.en: It's not just the metaphorical way, perhaps that we describe, uh, feeling like there's a hole in our heart.
sentences.zh: 这不仅仅是我们用来描述“感觉心像被掏空”的隐喻方式。

sentences.en: Um, and so with that, then we come to understand differently, perhaps, and can consider things like phantom limb syndrome, right?
sentences.zh: 嗯，因此，我们或许能以不同的方式去理解，并考虑像“幻肢综合征”这样的现象，对吧？

sentences.en: Where, where people who have had, uh, an arm or part of a leg amputated, they sometimes experience itching or pain in that absent limb.
sentences.zh: 那些截肢了手臂或部分腿部的人，有时会感觉到缺失的肢体有瘙痒或疼痛。

sentences.en: And, and we know it's because the brain has not rewired its representation of the body.
sentences.zh: 我们知道这是因为大脑还没有重新连接其身体表征。

sentences.en: And so we're actually experiencing sensations in the brain that aren't related to peripheral nerves.
sentences.zh: 所以我们实际上是在大脑中体验到与周围神经无关的感觉。

sentences.en: I think that we're coming to discover the way that we gets encoded might mean that we continue to expect to have both parts of we, uh, as we function in the world
sentences.zh: 我认为我们正在发现，“我们”被编码的方式可能意味着，当我们在这个世界上活动时，我们继续期望拥有“我们”的两个部分，

sentences.en: and, and then experience it as a, as a great loss, as a, as a missing, as an absence, uh, when, when they're not there, uh, with us.
sentences.zh: 然后当他们不在我们身边时，我们就会将其体验为一种巨大的损失，一种缺失，一种空虚。

sentences.en: And so is there a kind of rewiring then that happens in the brain after we lose someone?
sentences.zh: 那么，在我们失去某人之后，大脑中是否会发生一种重新连接？

sentences.en: There is.
sentences.zh: 是的。

sentences.en: And some of what we know about this is actually from the work of Zoe Donaldson at the University of Colorado Boulder.
sentences.zh: 我们对此的部分了解实际上来自科罗拉多大学博尔德分校的佐伊·唐纳森（Zoe Donaldson）的研究。

sentences.en: She studies voles, these little rodents who, who mate for life.
sentences.zh: 她研究田鼠，这些终身一夫一妻制的小啮齿动物。

sentences.en: Uh, and because they mate for life, it gives us an opportunity to really investigate from a neuroscience perspective, what happens then if, if, if a mate goes missing
sentences.zh: 因为它们终身配对，这让我们有机会从神经科学的角度真正研究：如果配偶失踪了，会发生什么？

sentences.en: in this volal couple?
sentences.zh: 在这对田鼠夫妇中。

sentences.en: And what we know is that there is extensive change in the brain when the bond is originally formed.
sentences.zh: 我们知道，当纽带最初形成时，大脑会发生广泛的变化。

sentences.en: There are changes to the way the proteins are folded in the, in the nucleus accumbens of the brain, this little part of the, of the reward network in the brain.
sentences.zh: 大脑伏隔核（大脑奖励网络中的这一小部分）中蛋白质的折叠方式发生了变化。

sentences.en: And then when time passes, there are these neurons that are devoted to firing when we approach a mate, right?
sentences.zh: 随着时间推移，大脑中会有专门负责在我们接近配偶时放电的神经元，对吧？

sentences.en: And as the bond grows stronger, we have more and more of these neurons just signifying how important it is that this function of, of seeking out our mate
sentences.zh: 随着纽带变得越来越强，我们拥有越来越多的神经元，这标志着寻找配偶的功能是多么重要，

sentences.en: and spending time with them gets so much resources of the brain.
sentences.zh: 并且花时间与他们在一起会占用大脑如此多的资源。

sentences.en: And then upon separation, we see all the physiological changes that happen.
sentences.zh: 然后，在分离时，我们看到了所有发生的生理变化。

sentences.en: the stress hormones that, um, that increase like cortisol or corticosterone in animals.
sentences.zh: 压力荷尔蒙，比如动物体内的皮质醇或皮质酮水平会升高。

sentences.en: And we see dopamine and oxytocin really trying to motivate us to find them again.
sentences.zh: 我们看到多巴胺和催产素确实在试图激励我们再次找到他们。

sentences.en: And over time, then there are neural and, um, transcriptional changes that happen in the brain as, as the, the voles try to understand what has happened.
sentences.zh: 随着时间推移，当田鼠试图理解发生了什么时，大脑中会发生神经和转录层面的变化。

sentences.en: And, and, uh, and the analogy then to humans, uh, although we have an additional two pounds of brain, so it's more complex certainly than for voles.
sentences.zh: 而与人类的类比，虽然我们的大脑多了两磅，所以肯定比田鼠复杂得多。

sentences.en: Uh, but nonetheless, I think we're seeing how, um, the brain has to really update and change and, and that that's partly a mechanical process and, and all of that takes time.
sentences.zh: 但尽管如此，我认为我们正在看到大脑必须如何真正更新和改变，这部分是一个机械过程，所有这些都需要时间。

sentences.en: So, much of your work is on what's called complicated grief.
sentences.zh: 所以，您的很多工作都是关于所谓的“复杂性悲伤”。

sentences.en: What's the difference between complicated grief and just everyday grief?
sentences.zh: 复杂性悲伤与日常悲伤有什么区别？

sentences.en: Yeah.
sentences.zh: 是的。

sentences.en: I like the term complicated grief, but I have to be honest with the listeners.
sentences.zh: 我喜欢“复杂性悲伤”这个词，但我必须对听众诚实。

sentences.en: The term that's been chosen by the DSM, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual, is prolonged grief disorder and that's been recently adopted actually within the last year.
sentences.zh: DSM（《精神疾病诊断与统计手册》）选择的术语是“迁延性悲伤障碍”，这实际上是最近一年内才采用的。

sentences.en: Um, the reason that I like the term complicated grief and really researchers are looking at the same phenomena when they, almost the same phenomena when they use both terms,
sentences.zh: 嗯，我喜欢“复杂性悲伤”这个词的原因是，研究人员在使用这两个术语时，几乎是在研究同一种现象，

sentences.en: but complicated grief to me reminds me that we're talking about complications.
sentences.zh: 但“复杂性悲伤”对我来说提醒我，我们谈论的是并发症。

sentences.en: So, here's an analogy that may help.
sentences.zh: 所以，这里有一个类比可能有所帮助。

sentences.en: If you break a bone, uh, we don't actually do something to knit those cells back together, right?
sentences.zh: 如果你骨折了，我们其实不会做些什么来把那些细胞重新缝合在一起，对吧？

sentences.en: That's a natural healing process that happens.
sentences.zh: 那是一个自然发生的愈合过程。

sentences.en: Although, we might do something to support that process.
sentences.zh: 虽然，我们可能会做些什么来支持这个过程。

sentences.en: So, we may wear a cast, for example, to give it support or use crutches, right, to, to give a little extra, uh, resources.
sentences.zh: 所以，我们可能会打石膏，比如给予支撑，或者使用拐杖，对吧，来提供一点额外的资源。

sentences.en: And that's a natural process unless sometimes we have complications where there's an infection in the area that's trying to heal or perhaps there's a secondary break in the bone.
sentences.zh: 这是一个自然过程，除非有时我们遇到并发症，比如愈合区域感染，或者骨头发生了二次骨折。

sentences.en: And under those circumstances, it can be very helpful for
sentences.zh: 在这种情况下，进行干预以帮助骨头回到其正常的愈合轨迹是非常有帮助的。

sentences.en: intervention to go in and help get that bone back on its typical healing trajectory.
sentences.zh: 所以，这个类比就是，我认为悲伤是对失去的自然反应。

sentences.en: So, the analogy then is that I think grief is a natural response to loss.
sentences.zh: 它就是我们的大脑、思维和身体在反应中所做的事情。

sentences.en: It just, it is what our brain, our mind, our body does in reaction.
sentences.zh: 我们绝大多数人都是非常有韧性的。

sentences.en: And the vast majority of us are quite resilient.
sentences.zh: 我们从乔治·博南诺（George Bonanno）的研究中得知，我们绝大多数人都会找到一种方法来恢复这种有意义的生活，找到一种方法，你知道，继续爱我们的孙辈，

sentences.en: We know from the work of George Bonanno that the vast majority of us will find a way to sort of restore this meaningful life, find a way to, you know, continue loving our grandkids
sentences.zh: 把晚餐端上桌，去杂货店购物，所有这些事情。

sentences.en: and getting dinner on the table and getting out to the grocery store, all those things.
sentences.zh: 困难在于我们在这个过程中可能会脱轨。

sentences.en: The difficulty comes when we can get derailed in that process.
sentences.zh: 而迁延性悲伤障碍以及为治疗它而开发的干预措施，确实专注于尝试为那些在自然悲伤过程中脱轨的人建立新技能，

sentences.en: And prolonged grief disorder and the interventions that have been developed to treat prolonged grief disorder really focus on trying to build new skills in a person who's been
sentences.zh: 通过使他们能够使用这些新技能回到愈合的轨道上。

sentences.en: derailed in their natural grieving process and by enabling them to use these new skills to get back on that healing trajectory.
sentences.zh: 所以，干预的目的不是让他们停止悲伤。

sentences.en: So, intervention is not designed to get them to stop grieving.
sentences.zh: 那不是目的。

sentences.en: That's not the idea.
sentences.zh: 而是去处理他们脱轨的方式，比如他们正在产生的特定想法，他们参与的那些在他们勇敢地试图向前迈进时并无帮助的行为。

sentences.en: But rather to take care of ways they become derailed, particular thoughts they're having, behaviors they're engaged in that are not helping as they're trying courageously to move
sentences.zh: 通过这种方式进行干预，我们现在知道，哥伦比亚大学凯西·希尔（Kathy Shear）所做的一些出色工作表明，

sentences.en: forward.
sentences.zh: 我们现在知道，对于患有迁延性悲伤障碍长达十年的患者，我们也可以进行有效干预，他们仍然能从这种心理治疗中受益。

sentences.en: And by intervening in this way, we know now some of the terrific work by
sentences.zh: 这只是引导人们以不同的方式思考吗？

sentences.en: Kathy Shear at Columbia
sentences.zh: 这就像认知行为疗法吗？

sentences.en: University, we know now that we can intervene effectively for folks who've had prolonged grief disorder for a decade, they still benefit from this type of psychotherapy.
sentences.zh: 你会得到一些练习来防止自己反刍吗？

sentences.en: And is it just directing people to think differently?
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，你试图对患有这种障碍的人做什么？

sentences.en: Is it like cognitive behavioral therapy?
sentences.zh: 在她开发的迁延性悲伤障碍治疗中，有几个不同的方面。

sentences.en: Are you given exercises to kind of keep you from ruminating?
sentences.zh: 这是一种手册化的疗法，它包括许多内容。

sentences.en: I mean, what are you trying to do with the person who has this disorder?
sentences.zh: 其中之一是真正专注于失去本身。

sentences.en: There are a few different aspects to it in prolonged grief disorder treatment that she has developed.
sentences.zh: 我们许多人，即使在谈论悲伤的感觉有多糟糕时，

sentences.en: It's a manualized therapy, and it includes a number of things.
sentences.zh: 那仍然与专注于死亡那一刻，或者当我们意识到这个人再也不会回来的那种终局性时的情况不同。

sentences.en: One of them is really focusing on the loss.
sentences.zh: 对于许多人来说，他们需要更多地接触那些记忆，才能真正理解发生了什么，以及他们如何理解这种体验。

sentences.en: Many of us, even when we talk about how awful grief feels,
sentences.zh: 所以他们会做一些我们可能认为是暴露疗法的事情，客户会谈论它并将其录下来，然后回听，同时培养如何进入悲伤情绪然后再次走出来的技能。

sentences.en: that's still different than focusing on what happened at the moment of death or when we realized the finality that this person just wasn't coming back.
sentences.zh: 培养围绕情绪调节的新技能，

sentences.en: For many people, they need more exposure to those memories to really understand what happened and how they understand
sentences.zh: 培养围绕接纳的新技能，

sentences.en: the experience.
sentences.zh: 但也包括其他方面。

sentences.en: So they'll do types of what we might recognize as exposure therapy, where clients will talk about it and have that recorded and then listen to it, while developing skills of how do
sentences.zh: 另一个方面不仅仅是关注失去，而是关注恢复你现在的生活是什么样的。

sentences.en: I move into the feeling of grief and then out of it again.
sentences.zh: 许多人因为悲伤太痛苦，开始回避与已故挚爱相关的环境、提醒或人。

sentences.en: Developing new skills around emotion regulation,
sentences.zh: 回避的问题在于它往往会蔓延，对吧？

sentences.en: developing skills around acceptance,
sentences.zh: 所以我们开始回避少数几件事，然后我们开始回避越来越多提醒我们这些痛苦悲伤感觉的事情。

sentences.en: but other things as well.
sentences.zh: 从大脑的角度来看，如果我们想了解现在的生活是什么样的，想了解什么对我们有意义，什么是有价值的，我们就必须参与到新的生活中去。

sentences.en: The other aspect isn't just focusing on the loss, but focusing on restoring what is life like for you now.
sentences.zh: 我们必须参与到新的生活中去。

sentences.en: Many people, because grief is so painful, have come to avoid situations or reminders or people associated with their deceased loved one.
sentences.zh: 我们必须参与到新的生活中去。

sentences.en: And the trouble with avoidance is it tends to spread, right?
sentences.zh: 我们必须参与到新的生活中去。

sentences.en: So we start avoiding a small number of things and then we start to avoid more and more things that remind us of these painful grief feelings.
sentences.zh: 我们必须参与到新的生活中去。

sentences.en: From the perspective of the brain, if we're going to learn what life is like now and we're going to learn what makes sense for us, what can be meaningful, we have to engage in new
sentences.zh: 我们必须参与到新的生活中去。

sentences.en: experiences.
sentences.zh: 经历。

sentences.en: That's how the brain learns.
sentences.zh: 大脑就是这样学习的。

sentences.en: And so the therapy helps to come up with possibilities, things that you might be avoiding and also things that you might try now.
sentences.zh: 因此，治疗有助于提出各种可能性，包括你可能一直在回避的事情，以及你现在可以尝试去做的事情。

sentences.en: And by giving people the support and encouragement, sometimes even permission, to engage in new behaviors, their brain does learn that life is full of many possibilities.
sentences.zh: 通过给予人们支持和鼓励，有时甚至给予他们许可去尝试新的行为，他们的大脑确实会认识到生活充满了无限可能。

sentences.en: And the final piece is really working with the support system of the person who's grieving so that they understand what this person is going through and that they can provide
sentences.zh: 最后一部分是真正与悲伤者的支持系统合作，让他们理解这个人正在经历什么，并能够提供

sentences.en: that sort of courageous support and also not back away from the intensity of the grieving person's feelings.
sentences.zh: 那种勇敢的支持，同时也不会因为悲伤者强烈的情绪而退缩。

sentences.en: So when many people think of grieving, what comes to mind is Elizabeth
sentences.zh: 所以，当许多人想到悲伤时，脑海中浮现的往往是伊丽莎白·

sentences.en: Kubler-Ross's five stages of grief, right?
sentences.zh: 库伯勒-罗斯的悲伤五个阶段，对吧？

sentences.en: Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and then finally acceptance.
sentences.zh: 否认、愤怒、讨价还价、抑郁，最后是接受。

sentences.en: But you've written that these stages aren't an accurate picture of how people grieve.
sentences.zh: 但你写过，这些阶段并不能准确反映人们悲伤的过程。

sentences.en: So how did the five stages become the standard of how we think of grieving and is there any part of that model that you believe makes sense?
sentences.zh: 那么，这五个阶段是如何成为我们思考悲伤的标准模式的？你认为该模型中是否有合理的部分？

sentences.en: Well, this is a great example I think of how making the distinction between grief and grieving can be so useful.
sentences.zh: 嗯，我认为这是一个很好的例子，说明区分“悲伤（grief）”和“哀伤（grieving）”是多么有用。

sentences.en: So I have just enormous respect for
sentences.zh: 我对伊丽莎白·

sentences.en: Dr. Elizabeth
sentences.zh: 库伯勒-罗斯博士怀有极大的敬意，

sentences.en: Kubler-Ross who's a psychiatrist working in the 1960s, a woman in her field when there were not many women in her field.
sentences.zh: 她是一位在20世纪60年代工作的精神科医生，在那个女性从业者寥寥无几的领域里，她是一位杰出的女性。

sentences.en: And she did what any good scientist does when they are working with a phenomena she described.
sentences.zh: 她做了任何优秀的科学家在研究某种现象时都会做的事情，她进行了描述。

sentences.en: Right?
sentences.zh: 对吧？

sentences.en: So she had this revolutionary idea that we could talk to terminally ill people that we could ask them what their experience was like.
sentences.zh: 她有一个革命性的想法，即我们可以与绝症患者交谈，可以询问他们的感受是怎样的。

sentences.en: And then she trained other medical residents and chaplains and social workers and psychologists and doctors to also talk with terminally ill people and find out what their grief
sentences.zh: 然后，她培训了其他住院医生、牧师、社会工作者、心理学家和医生，让他们也与绝症患者交谈，了解他们的悲伤

sentences.en: was like.
sentences.zh: 是什么样的。

sentences.en: And this was then also applied to bereaved people as well.
sentences.zh: 后来，这也应用到了丧亲者身上。

sentences.en: So she described grief in a very accurate way.
sentences.zh: 所以，她对悲伤的描述是非常准确的。

sentences.en: Anger is a part of grief, isn't it?
sentences.zh: 愤怒是悲伤的一部分，不是吗？

sentences.en: And depression is often a part of the feelings of grief.
sentences.zh: 而抑郁也往往是悲伤情绪的一部分。

sentences.en: What makes it difficult and we know now from some of the more recent work by
sentences.zh: 是什么让它变得困难呢？我们现在从杰森·霍兰德和鲍勃·

sentences.en: Jason Holland and Bob
sentences.zh: 杰森·霍兰德和鲍勃

sentences.en: B.
sentences.zh: 迈耶最近的一些研究中了解到，

sentences.en: Meyer who looked at the trajectory of grieving over time.
sentences.zh: 他们观察了哀伤随时间变化的轨迹。

sentences.en: So the difference between just what the moment felt like the anger, say for example, someone is expressing compared to how that anger might change if you interviewed the same
sentences.zh: 所以，仅仅是那一刻的感觉——比如某人表达的愤怒——与如果你在一年或几年内多次采访同一个人时，

sentences.en: person multiple times across a year or a couple of years of their life.
sentences.zh: 那种愤怒可能会如何改变，这两者之间是有区别的。

sentences.en: And so what we know now is that there isn't a linear process.
sentences.zh: 我们现在知道，这并不是一个线性的过程。

sentences.en: We don't do all of depression and then we get to all of acceptance, but rather over time research suggests that yearning declines and that acceptance increases, but that
sentences.zh: 我们不会先经历完所有的抑郁，然后就直接进入所有的接受阶段。相反，研究表明，随着时间的推移，渴望会减少，接受度会增加，但

sentences.en: this doesn't happen in a stair-step kind of way.
sentences.zh: 这并不是以阶梯式的方式发生的。

sentences.en: Rather, we know, for example, that at anniversaries or at the holidays, people tend to have a resurgence of grief.
sentences.zh: 相反，我们知道，例如在周年纪念日或节假日，人们往往会再次陷入悲伤。

sentences.en: And that doesn't mean that their grieving trajectory isn't still going in the right direction.
sentences.zh: 但这并不意味着他们的哀伤轨迹没有朝着正确的方向发展。

sentences.en: It just means that these are moments where people are aware of their grief.
sentences.zh: 这只是意味着在这些时刻，人们意识到了自己的悲伤。

sentences.en: So if we use it as a description,
sentences.zh: 所以，如果我们把它当作一种描述，

sentences.en: I think that that works well.
sentences.zh: 我认为这很有效。

sentences.en: If we use it as a prescription for how to grieve, I think it often doesn't fit people's experience and it doesn't mean their experience is wrong in any way.
sentences.zh: 但如果我们把它当作如何哀伤的处方，我认为它往往不符合人们的真实体验，但这并不意味着他们的体验有任何错误。

sentences.en: We recently had another episode with psychologist
sentences.zh: 我们最近邀请了心理学家

sentences.en: Dr.
sentences.zh: 保琳·

sentences.en: Pauline
sentences.zh: 博斯博士，

sentences.en: Boss, who was an expert on what she's termed ambiguous loss.
sentences.zh: 她是她所称的“模棱两可的失落”方面的专家。

sentences.en: That is loss where a loved one is physically absent, but there's no body, like a prisoner of war, or where a person is physically present, but mentally absent, as in dementia.
sentences.zh: 也就是说，亲人身体不在了，但没有遗体，比如战俘；或者人还在，但精神不在了，比如痴呆症患者。

sentences.en: Do our brains process ambiguous losses differently than they do a more clear cut loss like an actual death?
sentences.zh: 我们的大脑处理模棱两可的失落，是否与处理像实际死亡这样明确的失落方式不同？

sentences.en: It's such important work, and I think people really resonate with this idea of ambiguous loss because it is so challenging.
sentences.zh: 这是一项非常重要的工作，我认为人们确实对“模棱两可的失落”这个概念产生了共鸣，因为它太具挑战性了。

sentences.en: So as I described before, even in a very clear cut case where we were there when the person died, we already are dealing with sort of these two
sentences.zh: 正如我之前所描述的，即使在非常明确的情况下，比如我们在场目睹了某人的离世，我们已经在处理这两种

sentences.en: streams of information that are in conflict with each other.
sentences.zh: 相互冲突的信息流了。

sentences.en: So on the one hand, we have the memory of being at the bedside of knowing that this person has died.
sentences.zh: 一方面，我们有在床边陪伴的记忆，知道这个人已经去世了。

sentences.en: And on the other hand, because of this bond that we formed, the way that we encode attachment is that this person will always be here for me and I will always be here for them.
sentences.zh: 另一方面，由于我们建立的这种纽带，我们编码依恋的方式是：这个人永远会在我身边，我也永远会在他们身边。

sentences.en: And we don't actually have to be in someone's presence in order for us to have that attachment of belief, right?
sentences.zh: 而且，我们实际上并不需要身处某人的面前才能拥有那种依恋的信念，对吧？

sentences.en: You wouldn't be able to send your kids to school every day if you didn't know
sentences.zh: 如果你不深信每天结束时，

sentences.en: deeply at the end of the day that
sentences.zh: 孩子们晚上都会回到家，

sentences.en: they're all going to be back at home at night.
sentences.zh: 你就无法每天送他们去上学。

sentences.en: And so that attachment belief really doesn't rely on the presence of the person.
sentences.zh: 所以，那种依恋信念并不依赖于人的在场。

sentences.en: Well, even in a clear-cut case of grieving, these two things conflict initially, don't they?
sentences.zh: 那么，即使在明确的哀伤案例中，这两件事最初也是冲突的，不是吗？

sentences.en: We have a memory on the one hand and on the other hand, this is an everlasting relationship and the solution is just to go find them if they're not in our presence.
sentences.zh: 我们一方面有记忆，另一方面这又是一段永恒的关系，而解决办法就是如果他们不在我们身边，就去找到他们。

sentences.en: So that I think causes a lot of
sentences.zh: 所以我认为这导致了许多

sentences.en: disorientation and is part of why it takes so long to grieve.
sentences.zh: 迷失感，这也是为什么哀伤需要这么长时间的部分原因。

sentences.en: Now, if you add on top of all that difficulty and uncertainty where you don't have memories of that person, of seeing their body at a funeral, of having a gravesite to go to,
sentences.zh: 现在，如果再加上所有的困难和不确定性，比如你没有那个人的记忆，没有在葬礼上看到他们的遗体，没有可以去祭拜的墓地，

sentences.en: then it makes the grieving even more complex, even more disorienting, or potentially takes even longer.
sentences.zh: 那么这会让哀伤变得更加复杂，更加令人迷失，或者可能需要更长的时间。

sentences.en: So while I think that we experience the feelings of grief, just as we would in a case of clear-cut death,
sentences.zh: 所以，虽然我认为我们经历的悲伤感受，与在明确死亡案例中的感受是一样的，

sentences.en: there are all these additional layers that then come along with it.
sentences.zh: 但随之而来的还有所有这些额外的层面。

sentences.en: It's a little bit related in a sense that when people grieve about a celebrity who died, someone they greatly admired, it's not a physical loss in the same way because you didn't
sentences.zh: 这在某种意义上有点相关，当人们为去世的名人悲伤时，那些他们非常钦佩的人，这并不是同一种身体上的失落，因为你并没有

sentences.en: have an actual relationship with the person other than the one you had in your mind.
sentences.zh: 与那个人有实际的关系，除了你脑海中存在的那种关系。

sentences.en: And you've termed this parasocial grief.
sentences.zh: 你把这称为“准社会悲伤”。

sentences.en: How is it that we can feel intensity of grief with someone like that, a celebrity, someone we admired, who has passed away?
sentences.zh: 为什么我们能对那样的人，一个我们钦佩的、已经去世的名人，感到如此强烈的悲伤？

sentences.en: This is a fascinating phenomenon, isn't it?
sentences.zh: 这是一个迷人的现象，不是吗？

sentences.en: We see when someone who's a famous actor or a musician dies, just this outpouring of grief often, and it seems almost incomprehensible.
sentences.zh: 我们看到当一位著名的演员或音乐家去世时，往往会出现这种悲伤的宣泄，这似乎几乎令人难以理解。

sentences.en: How are these individuals who did not know this person so moved that they would come to a place and leave flowers and candles?
sentences.zh: 这些并不认识这个人的人，怎么会如此感动，以至于他们会来到某个地方留下鲜花和蜡烛？

sentences.en: And you even just hear people describe or perhaps have felt yourself that pang that really sticks with you when a celebrity or an actor or a musician has died.
sentences.zh: 你甚至会听到人们描述，或者你自己可能也感受过，当一位名人、演员或音乐家去世时，那种真正刺痛你的心酸感。

sentences.en: And I think it relates to exactly what you were saying.
sentences.zh: 我认为这和你刚才说的话完全相关。

sentences.en: While there's no official relationship that could be pointed to from the outside, and certainly we know that person doesn't know us.
sentences.zh: 虽然从外部看，并没有官方的联系，我们也确实知道那个人并不认识我们。

sentences.en: On the other hand, many of those art forms,
sentences.zh: 但另一方面，许多艺术形式，

sentences.en: they provide us a way to access some of our inner emotions.
sentences.zh: 它们为我们提供了一种进入内心深处情感的方式。

sentences.en: Think about the way musicians will write lyrics and we think, oh my goodness, how could they know that about me?
sentences.zh: 想想音乐家写歌词的方式，我们会想，天哪，他们怎么会知道我内心的想法？

sentences.en: That really describes exactly how I feel.
sentences.zh: 那真的准确描述了我的感受。

sentences.en: And I think that is a kind of bonding that happens.
sentences.zh: 我认为这是一种发生的联结。

sentences.en: And often these
sentences.zh: 而且通常这些

sentences.en: relationships,
sentences.zh: 关系，

sentences.en: I'll call them, these connections to actors and musicians happen at times in our life where we really are trying to find the words for how we feel inside.
sentences.zh: 我称之为与演员和音乐家的这种联系，往往发生在我们人生中真正试图为内心感受寻找词汇的时期。

sentences.en: So that time that we have spent binge watching an actor or spent time listening over and over and over again to music, I think in a sense that is a kind of bonding.
sentences.zh: 所以，我们花时间沉迷于观看某位演员的作品，或者一遍又一遍地听音乐，我认为在某种意义上，这是一种联结。

sentences.en: And therefore that parasocial grief means that we lose a person who really understood the way we see the world.
sentences.zh: 因此，那种准社会悲伤意味着我们失去了一个真正理解我们看待世界方式的人。

sentences.en: And we often associate that with a particular time in our life, right?
sentences.zh: 而且我们通常会将这种感觉与人生中的特定时期联系起来，对吧？

sentences.en: So if a musician dies that I listened to all through college,
sentences.zh: 所以如果我大学期间一直听的音乐家去世了，

sentences.en: I feel a little piece of my college self has gone as well that I'll never have again, you know?
sentences.zh: 我觉得我大学时期的那一小部分自我也随之消失了，我再也找不回来了，你知道吗？

sentences.en: Yeah, we're very nostalgic.
sentences.zh: 是的，我们非常怀旧。
